    if b == 0 {
        panic!("Division by zero!");
    }
    a / b
}

13.2.2 Panic Execution Flow

13.2.3 Stack Unwinding Details

fn level3() {
    panic!("error!");  // Call panic
}

fn level2() {
    let x = vec![1, 2, 3];  // Allocated
    level3();               // Panics
    // Drop x (called during unwind)
}

fn level1() {
    let s = String::from("test");  // Allocated
    level2();
    // Drop s (called during unwind)
}

// Unwind sequence:
// 1. panic!() called in level3
// 2. level3 frame exits (no locals to drop)
// 3. level2 frame exits (drop x: vec freed)
// 4. level1 frame exits (drop s: string freed)
// 5. main frame exits (process terminates)

13.3 2. Result<T, E> Representation

13.3.1 Result Enum

pub enum Result<T, E> {
    Ok(T),
    Err(E),
}

13.3.2 Result Memory Layout

13.3.3 Result Size

println!("{}", std::mem::size_of::<Result<i32, String>>());    // 32
println!("{}", std::mem::size_of::<Result<(), String>>());     // 24 (no Ok payload)
println!("{}", std::mem::size_of::<Result<i32, ()>>());        // 8 (niche optimization)

13.4 3. Option as Special Case of Result

13.4.1 Option Representation

pub enum Option<T> {
    Some(T),
    None,
}

13.4.2 Niche Optimization in Result

// Without niche optimization:
// Result<&T, ()> would be 16 bytes (pointer + tag)

// With niche optimization:
// Result<&T, ()> is 8 bytes (null = Err, non-null = Ok)

println!("{}", std::mem::size_of::<Result<&i32, ()>>());  // 8 (not 16!)

Niche = unused discriminant value in the type itself

13.5 4. The ? Operator (Question Mark)

13.5.1 Short-Circuit Error Propagation

fn parse_config(s: &str) -> Result<Config, Error> {
    let a = parse_a(s)?;      // If Err, return immediately
    let b = parse_b(s)?;      // If Err, return immediately
    let c = parse_c(s)?;      // If Err, return immediately
    Ok(Config { a, b, c })    // All succeeded
}

13.5.2 ? Desugaring

// This:
let x = some_result?;

// Desugars to:
let x = match some_result {
    Ok(val) => val,
    Err(err) => return Err(err),
};

13.5.3 Error Type Conversion

fn example() -> Result<(), CustomError> {
    let _file = std::fs::File::open("test.txt")?;  // IoError → CustomError (via From)
    Ok(())
}

// ? performs .into() conversion:
// IoError → CustomError (if impl From<IoError> for CustomError)

13.6 5. Panic Modes: Unwind vs Abort

13.6.1 Unwind (Default)

// Cargo.toml
[profile.release]
panic = "unwind"  // Stack unwinding

// If panic occurs:
// 1. Unwind stack
// 2. Call drop() on all locals
// 3. Terminate

13.6.2 Abort

// Cargo.toml
[profile.release]
panic = "abort"  // Immediate termination

// If panic occurs:
// 1. Immediately crash
// 2. No unwinding
// 3. Faster, smaller binary

Performance trade-off: - Unwind: Slower (cleanup code), larger binary - Abort: Faster, smaller binary, but no cleanup

13.7 6. Catching Panics

13.7.1 catch_unwind (Advanced)

use std::panic;

let result = panic::catch_unwind(|| {
    // Code that might panic
    let x = 42 / 0;  // Would panic
});

match result {
    Ok(val) => println!("Success: {}", val),
    Err(_) => println!("Caught panic!"),
}

13.7.2 Panic Unwinding with catch_unwind

13.8 7. Panic Handling in Threads

13.8.1 Thread Panic

use std::thread;

let handle = thread::spawn(|| {
    panic!("error in thread");
});

// Main thread continues
match handle.join() {
    Ok(_) => println!("Thread succeeded"),
    Err(_) => println!("Thread panicked"),
}

13.8.2 Thread Isolation

13.9 8. Error Types and From/Into

13.9.1 Standard Error Trait

pub trait Error: Debug + Display {
    fn source(&self) -> Option<&(dyn Error + 'static)> {
        None
    }
}

13.9.2 Error Conversion with From

impl From<std::io::Error> for MyError {
    fn from(e: std::io::Error) -> Self {
        MyError::Io(e)
    }
}

// ? operator uses this:
let file = std::fs::File::open("test.txt")?;  // IoError auto-converted

13.10 9. Panic vs Result Semantics

13.10.1 When to Panic

// Acceptable panics:
assert!(condition);        // Assertions in tests
unwrap();                  // "I know this is safe"
expect("message");         // Documented assumption
panic!("unreachable");     // Genuinely impossible state

// In library code: rarely panic
// In application code: more acceptable

13.10.2 When to Use Result

// Operations that might reasonably fail:
fn parse(s: &str) -> Result<Config, ParseError> { ... }
fn open_file(path: &str) -> Result<File, IoError> { ... }
fn fetch_data(url: &str) -> Result<Data, NetworkError> { ... }

13.11 10. Double-Ended Error Handling

13.11.1 Panics at Type Boundaries

fn api_function(x: &str) -> i32 {
    // Internal: can panic for assertions
    assert!(!x.is_empty(), "x must be non-empty");
    
    // Or return Result for recoverable errors
    let val: i32 = x.parse()?;
    Ok(val)
}

13.11.2 Error Pyramid

13.12 11. Panic Information

13.12.1 Panic Hook

use std::panic;

panic::set_hook(Box::new(|panic_info| {
    println!("Panic occurred: {}", panic_info);
    
    if let Some(location) = panic_info.location() {
        println!("At {}:{}", location.file(), location.line());
    }
}));

panic!("Custom panic!");

13.12.2 Panic Location in Binary

fn my_function() {
    panic!("here!");  // Line 5, Column 5
    // Location stored in binary (requires debug info)
}

13.13 12. Performance Implications

13.13.1 Zero-Cost Result

// Result<T, E> has minimal overhead:
fn operation() -> Result<i32, Error> {
    let result = some_computation();
    if result < 0 {
        Err(NegativeError)
    } else {
        Ok(result)
    }
}

// Compiles to simple conditional + return
// No allocation, no exception handling (except panics)

13.13.2 Panic Cost

Panic (abort): 0 cycles (process exits immediately)
Panic (unwind): 100+ cycles (unwind stack, drop locals)

13.14 13. Result Combinators

13.14.1 map, and_then, unwrap_or

let result: Result<i32, &str> = Ok(10);

// Transform value
result.map(|x| x * 2);                      // Ok(20)

// Chain operations
result.and_then(|x| Ok(x * 2));             // Ok(20)

// Provide default
result.unwrap_or(0);                         // 10
result.unwrap_or_else(|_| 0);               // 10

13.15 14. Error Propagation Patterns

13.15.1 Accumulate Errors

fn validate_all(data: &Data) -> Result<(), Vec<Error>> {
    let mut errors = Vec::new();
    
    if !valid_a(&data.a) {
        errors.push(Error::A);
    }
    if !valid_b(&data.b) {
        errors.push(Error::B);
    }
    
    if errors.is_empty() {
        Ok(())
    } else {
        Err(errors)
    }
}

13.16 Summary

Aspect Panic Result
Recovery No (terminates) Yes (explicit)
Type Unwind token Enum (Ok/Err)
Overhead Unwind cost None (zero-cost)
When Invariants violated Expected failures
Propagation Stack unwind ? operator

Next: Pattern Matching → Learn match compilation and exhaustiveness checking.

14 Pattern Matching: Compilation to Jump Tables and Exhaustiveness

14.1 Overview

Pattern matching is a first-class feature in Rust. The compiler transforms match expressions into efficient jump tables or decision trees, ensuring exhaustiveness at compile-time while generating optimal machine code.

14.2 1. Match Expression Compilation

14.2.1 Simple Match

let x = 2;
match x {
    1 => println!("one"),
    2 => println!("two"),
    3 => println!("three"),
    _ => println!("other"),
}

14.2.2 Compilation Strategy

The compiler chooses between: 1. Jump table - O(1) dispatch (for small integer ranges) 2. Decision tree - O(log n) comparisons (for sparse ranges) 3. Direct comparison - O(n) comparisons (for small match arms)

14.2.3 Jump Table (Typical)

14.3 2. Enum Pattern Matching

14.3.1 Discriminant-based Dispatch

enum Color {
    Red,
    Green,
    Blue,
}

match color {
    Color::Red => ...,
    Color::Green => ...,
    Color::Blue => ...,
}

14.3.2 Discriminant Values

// Internal representation (simplified):
enum Color {
    Red = 0,       // discriminant 0
    Green = 1,     // discriminant 1
    Blue = 2,      // discriminant 2
}

// Compiler reads discriminant from memory
// Jumps to corresponding arm

14.3.3 Result/Option Pattern Matching

match result {
    Ok(val) => process(val),    // discriminant 0
    Err(e) => handle_error(e),  // discriminant 1
}

Discriminants stored inline in the enum data.

14.4 3. Struct Pattern Matching

14.4.1 Destructuring Fields

struct Point {
    x: i32,
    y: i32,
}

match point {
    Point { x: 0, y: 0 } => println!("origin"),
    Point { x: 0, y } => println!("y-axis: {}", y),
    Point { x, y } => println!("({}, {})", x, y),
}

14.4.2 Compilation Strategy: Decision Tree

14.5 4. Guard Clauses

14.5.1 Adding Conditions

match x {
    n if n % 2 == 0 => println!("even"),
    n if n > 10 => println!("odd and > 10"),
    _ => println!("other"),
}

14.5.2 Compilation

Jump to discriminant arm (if simple enum)
↓
Evaluate guard condition
↓
If true: execute arm
If false: continue to next arm (or default)

14.6 5. Exhaustiveness Checking

14.6.1 Compiler Ensures All Cases

let x: Option<i32> = Some(42);

// ERROR: match not exhaustive
match x {
    Some(n) => println!("{}", n),
    // Missing: None case
}

// FIXED: handle all cases
match x {
    Some(n) => println!("{}", n),
    None => println!("no value"),
}

14.6.2 How Exhaustiveness Works

// Compiler builds a decision tree:
// 1. All possible values? → all branches covered
// 2. Missing case? → compiler error

match (x, y) {
    (0, 0) => {},
    (0, _) => {},
    (_, 0) => {},
    (_, _) => {},
}
// All combinations covered ✓

match (x, y) {
    (0, 0) => {},
    (0, _) => {},
    // Missing: (non-0, 0) and (non-0, non-0) → ERROR
}

14.7 6. Never Pattern and Unreachable

14.7.1 Impossible Cases

enum Infallible {}  // No variants

match infallible {
    // Exhaustive (no cases possible)
}

14.7.2 Unreachable Arms

match x {
    1 => println!("one"),
    _ => println!("other"),
    1 => println!("never reached!"),  // ERROR: unreachable pattern
}

14.8 7. Performance of Match vs If-Else

14.8.1 Switch-like (Jump Table)

match x {
    0 => a(),
    1 => b(),
    2 => c(),
    _ => d(),
}

Compiled to: - Jump table lookup: O(1) - Branch prediction friendly - CPU cache efficient

14.8.2 If-Else Chain

if x == 0 {
    a()
} else if x == 1 {
    b()
} else if x == 2 {
    c()
} else {
    d()
}

Compiled to: - Multiple comparisons: O(n) worst case - Branch prediction less friendly - Slower on average

Result: Match is typically faster.

14.9 8. Pattern Matching on Slices

14.9.1 Slice Patterns

match arr {
    [] => println!("empty"),
    [a] => println!("single: {}", a),
    [a, b] => println!("pair: {} {}", a, b),
    [a, .., b] => println!("first and last: {} {}", a, b),
    _ => println!("many"),
}

14.9.2 Compilation: Bounds Check + Dispatch

1. Check array length
2. Jump to corresponding arm
3. Extract pattern bindings

14.10 9. Or Patterns

match x {
    1 | 2 | 3 => println!("1-3"),
    4..=6 => println!("4-6"),
    _ => println!("other"),
}

14.10.1 Compilation

Or patterns merged into single jump table entry:
  table[1] = arm1_handler
  table[2] = arm1_handler  (same as 1)
  table[3] = arm1_handler  (same as 1)
  table[4..=6] = arm2_handler

14.11 10. Binding and Move Semantics

14.11.1 Patterns Capture Values

match result {
    Ok(value) => println!("{}", value),  // value moved from Ok
    Err(e) => println!("error: {}", e),  // e moved from Err
}
// result consumed (moved)

14.11.2 Reference Patterns

match &result {  // Match reference
    Ok(value) => println!("{}", value),   // value is &T
    Err(e) => println!("error: {}", e),   // e is &E
}
// result NOT consumed

14.11.3 Mutable Reference Patterns

match &mut result {
    Ok(value) => *value += 1,  // Can mutate through &mut
    Err(_) => {},
}

14.12 11. Nested Patterns

14.12.1 Deep Matching

match point {
    Point { x: Point { x: 0, y: 0 }, y: 0 } => ...,
    Point { x, y: 0 } if x > 0 => ...,
    _ => ...,
}

14.12.2 Decision Tree Depth

  • Each pattern adds a level
  • Deeply nested patterns = deeper decision tree
  • More branches = larger code size (code bloat)

14.13 12. Match Expression as Value

14.13.1 Returning Values

let value = match x {
    1 => "one",
    2 => "two",
    _ => "other",
};

// All arms must return same type
// Type checked at compile time

14.13.2 With Side Effects

let result = match config {
    Config::A => {
        println!("Running A");
        expensive_operation_a()
    },
    Config::B => {
        println!("Running B");
        expensive_operation_b()
    },
};

14.14 13. Exhaustiveness Algorithm

14.14.1 Compiler’s Approach

Given match arms:
1. Build set of all possible values (type)
2. Subtract covered patterns (union of all arms)
3. If remainder non-empty → ERROR: non-exhaustive
4. If remainder empty → OK: exhaustive

14.14.2 Example with Result<T, E>

enum Result<T, E> {
    Ok(T),    // variant 0
    Err(E),   // variant 1
}

match result {
    Ok(v) => ...,   // covers variant 0
    Err(e) => ...,  // covers variant 1
}
// All variants covered ✓

14.15 14. Performance Metrics

14.15.1 Benchmark

Jump table dispatch: 1-2 CPU cycles
Decision tree dispatch: 2-5 CPU cycles (depending on depth)
If-else chain: 1-10 CPU cycles (branch mispredictions)

14.15.2 Code Generation

// With -O (release):
match x {
    0..=10 => cmp + jmp table      // 1 instruction
    _ => jmp default
}

// Naive if-else:
if x == 0 { ... }
else if x == 1 { ... }
...
// 20 instructions for 10 comparisons

14.16 Summary Diagram

Next: Trait Objects → Learn polymorphism, fat pointers, and casting.

15 Trait Objects: Fat Pointers, Polymorphism, and Dynamic Dispatch

15.1 Overview

Trait objects enable runtime polymorphism through dynamic dispatch. Implemented as fat pointers (data pointer + virtual table pointer), they allow calling methods on unknown concrete types.

15.2 1. Static vs Dynamic Dispatch

15.2.1 Static Dispatch (Generics)

fn process<T: Drawable>(item: T) {
    item.draw();  // Resolved at compile time
}

process(circle);    // Generates code for Circle::draw
process(square);    // Generates code for Square::draw

Result: Separate function for each type (monomorphization).

15.2.2 Dynamic Dispatch (Trait Objects)

fn process(item: &dyn Drawable) {
    item.draw();  // Resolved at runtime via vtable
}

process(&circle);   // Same function for all types
process(&square);   // Looks up method in vtable

Result: Single function, method lookup via pointer.

15.3 2. Trait Object Creation

15.3.1 Type Erasure

trait Animal {
    fn speak(&self);
}

impl Animal for Dog {
    fn speak(&self) { println!("Woof!"); }
}

impl Animal for Cat {
    fn speak(&self) { println!("Meow!"); }
}

let dog: Box<dyn Animal> = Box::new(Dog);  // Type erased
let cat: &dyn Animal = &Cat;               // Type erased

15.3.2 Boxing into Trait Objects

let animals: Vec<Box<dyn Animal>> = vec![
    Box::new(Dog),
    Box::new(Cat),
];

for animal in animals {
    animal.speak();  // Dispatches to correct implementation
}

15.4 3. Fat Pointer Structure

15.4.1 Trait Object Representation

15.4.2 Box Layout

println!("{}", std::mem::size_of::<Box<dyn Animal>>());  // 16 bytes
println!("{}", std::mem::size_of::<&dyn Animal>());      // 16 bytes

// Compare:
println!("{}", std::mem::size_of::<Box<Dog>>());         // 8 bytes
println!("{}", std::mem::size_of::<&Dog>());             // 8 bytes

15.5 4. Virtual Table (vtable)

15.5.1 VTable Structure

15.5.2 VTable Creation (Compile-Time)

// For Dog implementing Animal:
const DOG_VTABLE: &VTable = &VTable {
    drop_glue: <Dog as Drop>::drop,
    size: std::mem::size_of::<Dog>(),
    align: std::mem::align_of::<Dog>(),
    speak: <Dog as Animal>::speak,
};

// For Cat implementing Animal:
const CAT_VTABLE: &VTable = &VTable {
    drop_glue: <Cat as Drop>::drop,
    size: std::mem::size_of::<Cat>(),
    align: std::mem::align_of::<Cat>(),
    speak: <Cat as Animal>::speak,
};

15.6 5. Method Dispatch

15.6.1 Calling Through Trait Object

let animal: &dyn Animal = &dog;
animal.speak();

15.6.2 Dispatch Sequence

15.6.3 Assembly-Like Pseudocode

; Load trait object (16 bytes)
mov rax, [trait_obj]        ; rax = data_ptr
mov rcx, [trait_obj + 8]    ; rcx = vtable_ptr

; Call method
mov r11, [rcx + 24]         ; r11 = vtable.speak (offset 24)
call r11                     ; Call speak(&dog_instance)

15.7 6. Object Safety

15.7.1 Requirements for Trait Objects

// Object-safe trait: ✓
trait Animal {
    fn speak(&self);
}

// NOT object-safe: ✗ (returns Self)
trait Cloneable {
    fn clone(&self) -> Self;  // ERROR: can't return dyn Trait
}

// NOT object-safe: ✗ (takes Self)
trait Movable {
    fn move_it(self);  // ERROR: can't consume dyn Trait
}

15.7.2 Why Not Object-Safe?

// This would be impossible:
let animal: &dyn Animal = &dog;
let cloned = animal.clone();  // What type is cloned?
                              // We don't know!

Trait object requires: all methods can work on &dyn Trait (or &mut).

15.8 7. Upcasting and Downcasting

15.8.1 Upcasting (Safe)

let dog: Dog = Dog;
let animal: &dyn Animal = &dog;  // Upcast (always safe)

15.8.2 Downcasting (Unsafe)

use std::any::Any;

let animal: &dyn Any = &dog;

if let Some(dog) = animal.downcast_ref::<Dog>() {
    println!("It's a dog!");
}

15.8.3 Downcast Sequence

15.9 8. Performance Cost of Dynamic Dispatch

15.9.1 Method Call Overhead

Static dispatch (inline):
call Dog::speak
(function address known, CPU can inline)

Dynamic dispatch (vtable):
mov rax, [vtable]           ; Load vtable
mov rcx, [rax + offset]     ; Load method pointer
call rcx                    ; Indirect call (1-2 cycle penalty)

Cost: 1-2 CPU cycles per method call (cache misses possible).

15.9.2 Benchmark

Direct call: 1 ns
Virtual call: 3-5 ns (3-5× overhead for small methods)

15.10 9. Trait Object with Associated Types

15.10.1 Associated Types Not Object-Safe

trait Container {
    type Item;
    fn get(&self) -> Self::Item;
}

// Can't create trait object (Item type unknown)
let c: Box<dyn Container> = Box::new(...);  // ERROR

Reason: Associated type must be concrete, but type erased.

15.11 10. Trait Objects and Ownership

15.11.1 Box

let animal: Box<dyn Animal> = Box::new(Dog);
// Box owns Dog
// When Box dropped, Dog dropped

drop(animal);  // Dog cleaned up via drop_glue

15.11.2 Reference &dyn Trait

let dog = Dog;
let animal: &dyn Animal = &dog;

// &dyn Animal doesn't own Dog
// Dog must live longer than reference

15.12 11. VTable Encoding

15.12.1 Type Information in VTable

// VTable contains:
struct VTable {
    drop_fn: unsafe fn(*mut ()),      // Drop implementation
    size: usize,                       // Size of concrete type
    align: usize,                      // Alignment
    
    // Method pointers (in declaration order)
    method1: unsafe fn(*const ()),
    method2: unsafe fn(*const (), i32),
    // ... more methods
}

15.12.2 Multiple Trait Objects

trait A { fn a(&self); }
trait B { fn b(&self); }

impl A for Dog { fn a(&self) { ... } }
impl B for Dog { fn b(&self) { ... } }

let a: &dyn A = &dog;  // VTable for A
let b: &dyn B = &dog;  // VTable for B (different)

// Two different trait objects for same Dog!

15.13 12. Combining Multiple Traits

15.13.1 Supertraits

trait Animal: Drawable + Named {
    fn speak(&self);
}

impl Animal for Dog {
    fn speak(&self) { println!("Woof"); }
}

// Dog must implement Drawable + Named too
let animal: &dyn Animal = &dog;  // VTable includes methods from Drawable, Named

15.13.2 Trait Object with Multiple Bounds

fn process(item: &(dyn Animal + Send + Sync)) {
    // Can call Animal methods
    // Guaranteed to be Send + Sync
}

15.14 13. Example: Polymorphic Vec

trait Command {
    fn execute(&mut self);
}

struct Commands(Vec<Box<dyn Command>>);

impl Commands {
    fn run(&mut self) {
        for cmd in &mut self.0 {
            cmd.execute();  // Dispatch through vtable
        }
    }
}

15.14.1 Memory Layout

15.15 14. Comparison: Static vs Dynamic

15.16 Summary

Aspect Trait Object Generic
Dispatch Dynamic (runtime) Static (compile-time)
Fat Pointer 16 bytes (ptr + vtable) N/A
Type Erasure Yes No
Code Size Smaller Larger (monomorphization)
Speed Slightly slower Faster (inlining)
Object Safety Required N/A

Next: Concurrency & Threading → Learn threads, channels, atomics, memory ordering.

16 Async/Await & Futures: State Machines Under the Hood

16.1 Overview

async/await is syntactic sugar for state machines. The compiler transforms async functions into types implementing the Future trait. Understanding this transformation is key to knowing why async is zero-cost and how it enables high-concurrency.

16.2 1. Futures: The Foundation

16.2.1 What is a Future?

A Future is a value that will eventually produce a result:

pub trait Future {
    type Output;

    fn poll(mut self: Pin<&mut Self>, cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<Self::Output>;
}

pub enum Poll<T> {
    Ready(T),
    Pending,
}

Semantics: - poll() - tries to make progress toward completion - Poll::Ready(T) - computation completed, here’s the result - Poll::Pending - not ready yet, call poll() again later

16.3 2. Async Functions as State Machines

16.3.1 Simple Async Function

async fn fetch_data() -> String {
    let data = get_from_network().await;
    process(data).await
}

16.3.2 Compiler Transformation

The compiler transforms the above into:

Generated state machine (conceptual):

enum FetchDataFuture {
    Start,
    AwaitingNetwork {
        future: GetFromNetworkFuture,
    },
    Processing {
        data: String,
        future: ProcessFuture,
    },
    Done,
}

impl Future for FetchDataFuture {
    type Output = String;

    fn poll(mut self: Pin<&mut Self>, cx: &mut Context) -> Poll<String> {
        match self {
            FetchDataFuture::Start => {
                // Initialize, transition to AwaitingNetwork
                *self = FetchDataFuture::AwaitingNetwork { future: ... };
                self.poll(cx)  // Poll again
            },
            FetchDataFuture::AwaitingNetwork { ref mut future } => {
                match Pin::new(future).poll(cx) {
                    Poll::Pending => Poll::Pending,
                    Poll::Ready(data) => {
                        *self = FetchDataFuture::Processing { data, future: ... };
                        self.poll(cx)
                    }
                }
            },
            FetchDataFuture::Processing { ref mut future, ... } => {
                match Pin::new(future).poll(cx) {
                    Poll::Pending => Poll::Pending,
                    Poll::Ready(result) => {
                        *self = FetchDataFuture::Done;
                        Poll::Ready(result)
                    }
                }
            },
            FetchDataFuture::Done => panic!("polled after completion"),
        }
    }
}

16.4 3. Await Points and Suspension

16.4.1 How Await Works

async fn example() {
    let x = some_async_op().await;  // Await point
    println!("{}", x);
}

At compile time: 1. Convert to state machine 2. Each await is a state transition point 3. Suspend = return Poll::Pending 4. Resume = poll() called again from same state

16.4.2 State Machine Memory Layout

16.5 4. The Executor Model

16.5.1 How Futures Get Polled

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let future = async {
        println!("Hello");
    };
    // Tokio executor polls the future to completion
}

Execution flow:

16.6 5. Pin and Unpin

16.6.1 Why Pin Exists

Async state machines contain self-referential data:

// Example: state machine with pointer to itself
enum MyFuture {
    State {
        data: String,
        ptr_to_data: *const String,  // Points to field above!
    },
}

// If we move the struct, the pointer becomes invalid!
// Pin prevents moving after first poll()

16.6.2 Pin Semantics

pub struct Pin<P> {
    pointer: P,  // Pointer to data
    // Promises data won't move
}

// Can't move if pinned
let mut future = async { ... };
let pinned = Pin::new(&mut future);
// Future must not move after this point!

16.6.3 Unpin Trait

pub auto trait Unpin {}  // Most types implement Unpin

// Types that don't implement Unpin:
// - Futures with self-references
// - Types with PhantomPinned

16.7 6. Context and Wakers

16.7.1 Context

pub fn poll(mut self: Pin<&mut Self>, cx: &mut Context) -> Poll<Output>;

Context contains: - Waker - tells executor to poll this future again

16.7.2 Waker

// When waiting for I/O:
pub trait Waker {
    fn wake(&self);  // Tell executor: "I'm ready now!"
}

// In future implementation:
fn poll(mut self: Pin<&mut Self>, cx: &mut Context) -> Poll<T> {
    // Register waker with I/O system
    io_system.register_callback(cx.waker().clone());
    Poll::Pending  // Not ready yet
    // When I/O completes, io_system calls waker.wake()
    // Executor polls this future again
}

Notification flow:

16.8 7. Async Function Transformation

16.8.1 Simple Example

async fn greet() -> String {
    "Hello".to_string()
}

Transforms into:

fn greet() -> impl Future<Output = String> {
    struct GreetFuture;

    impl Future for GreetFuture {
        type Output = String;

        fn poll(self: Pin<&mut Self>, _cx: &mut Context) -> Poll<String> {
            Poll::Ready("Hello".to_string())
        }
    }

    GreetFuture
}

16.8.2 With Await

async fn fetch_and_greet() -> String {
    let greeting = greet().await;
    format!("{}, World!", greeting)
}

Transforms into state machine (similar to earlier example).

16.9 8. Move Semantics in Async

16.9.1 Capturing Variables

let name = "Alice".to_string();

let future = async {
    println!("Hello, {}", name);  // Captures name
};

Closure behavior: - Immutable closure if only read - Mutable closure if modified - Consumes (moves) if needed

The state machine captures name as a field.

16.9.2 Problematic Move

async fn problem() {
    let x = vec![1, 2, 3];
    let fut = async {
        drop(x);  // Future owns x (moved)
    };
    // x no longer available here - moved into fut
}

16.10 9. Async/Await Performance

16.10.1 Zero-Cost Abstraction

// This:
async fn work() {
    a().await;
    b().await;
}

// Compiles roughly to:
fn work() -> impl Future {
    // State machine with states for each await point
    // No heap allocation by default (stack-based)
    // Calls functions directly (no indirection)
}

Cost: Only the state machine enum size (typically hundreds of bytes) + actual computation.

16.10.2 Benchmark

Sync function call: 1-2 cycles
Async function poll: 1-2 cycles (same!)
Overhead: Only when awaiting on I/O

16.11 10. Cancellation and Drop

16.11.1 Dropping a Future

async fn long_task() {
    // Some work
}

let future = long_task();
drop(future);  // Drops the entire state machine
               // Cleans up any resources

The state machine’s Drop impl cleans up nested futures and resources.

16.11.2 Cancellation Safety

select! {
    _ = fut1 => {},
    _ = fut2 => {},
}
// One future may be dropped mid-execution!

Futures must implement cancellation-safe cleanup.

16.12 11. Common Async Patterns

16.12.1 Spawn Task

tokio::spawn(async {
    // Runs independently
});

16.12.2 Race Futures

tokio::select! {
    res1 = future1 => { ... }
    res2 = future2 => { ... }
}

16.12.3 Join Futures

let (res1, res2) = tokio::join!(future1, future2);

16.13 12. Heap Allocation in Async

16.13.1 Stack vs Heap

// Stack (preferred):
async fn stack_based() {
    let fut = simple_future();  // Stack-based state machine
    fut.await;
}

// Heap (when needed):
async fn heap_based() {
    let fut = Box::new(large_future());  // On heap
    fut.await;
}

Most async code is stack-based (no heap allocation).

16.14 Summary Diagram

Next: Tokio Runtime → Learn event-driven I/O architecture.

17 Concurrency: Threads, Channels, Atomics, Memory Ordering Under the Hood

17.1 Overview

Rust’s concurrency model guarantees thread safety through Send/Sync traits and memory safety through ownership. Synchronization primitives (channels, atomics) build on these foundations to coordinate work across threads.

17.2 1. Threads and OS-Level Parallelism

17.2.1 Creating Threads

use std::thread;

thread::spawn(|| {
    println!("Hello from thread");
});

// Main thread continues

17.2.2 Thread Lifecycle

17.2.3 Stack Allocation

let handle = thread::spawn(|| {
    // New OS thread created
    // Stack allocated: ~2 MB (Linux typical)
    // Stack pointer initialized
    // closure executed within this stack
});

handle.join().expect("Thread panicked");  // Wait for completion

17.3 2. Send and Sync Traits

17.3.1 Send Trait

pub trait Send: Sized {}
// T: Send if ownership can be transferred across threads

// Example: String is Send
fn use_in_thread<T: Send>(t: T) {
    thread::spawn(move || {
        println!("{:?}", t);  // t moved into thread
    });
}

17.3.2 Sync Trait

pub trait Sync: Sized {}
// T: Sync if &T can be shared between threads safely

// Example: Arc<T> is Sync if T: Send + Sync
fn use_shared<T: Sync>(t: &T) {
    thread::spawn(move || {
        println!("{:?}", t);  // &t shared with thread
    });
}

17.3.3 Common Types

17.4 3. Channels: MPSC Communication

17.4.1 Channel Creation

use std::sync::mpsc;

let (tx, rx) = mpsc::channel();

thread::spawn(move || {
    tx.send(42).unwrap();  // Send value through channel
});

let value = rx.recv().unwrap();  // Receive on main thread
println!("{}", value);

17.4.2 Channel Architecture

17.4.3 Blocking Semantics

// Sender blocks if channel full (bounded channel)
let (tx, rx) = mpsc::channel::<i32>();  // Unbounded
let (tx, rx) = mpsc::sync_channel(10);   // Bounded (max 10 messages)

tx.send(value)?;  // Blocks if 10 messages queued

// Receiver blocks until message available
rx.recv()?;  // Blocks
rx.try_recv()?;  // Non-blocking (returns Err if empty)

17.5 4. Multiple Producers

17.5.1 Cloning Senders

let (tx, rx) = mpsc::channel();

let tx1 = tx.clone();
let tx2 = tx.clone();

thread::spawn(move || {
    tx1.send(1).unwrap();
});

thread::spawn(move || {
    tx2.send(2).unwrap();
});

while let Ok(val) = rx.recv() {
    println!("{}", val);  // Receives 1 and 2
}

17.5.2 Reference Counting

Initial: Sender count = 1
Clone 1: Sender count = 2
Clone 2: Sender count = 3
...
Drop all clones: count = 0
Receiver.recv() returns Err (channel closed)

17.6 5. Atomics: Lock-Free Synchronization

17.6.1 AtomicU32

use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicU32, Ordering};

let counter = AtomicU32::new(0);

thread::spawn(|| {
    counter.fetch_add(1, Ordering::SeqCst);  // Atomic increment
});

thread::spawn(|| {
    counter.fetch_add(1, Ordering::SeqCst);  // Atomic increment
});

// Result: 2 (no race condition)

17.6.2 Atomic Size

println!("{}", std::mem::size_of::<AtomicU32>());  // 4 (same as u32)
println!("{}", std::mem::size_of::<AtomicU64>());  // 8 (same as u64)

17.6.3 Atomic Operations

17.7 6. Memory Ordering

17.7.1 Ordering Options

17.7.2 Ordering Semantics

use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicU32, Ordering::*};

let data = AtomicU32::new(0);

// Relaxed: no barrier
data.store(42, Relaxed);           // No synchronization

// Release: write barrier
data.store(42, Release);           // Other threads see all prior writes

// Acquire: read barrier
let val = data.load(Acquire);      // Ensure all later reads see this

// SeqCst: sequential consistency
data.store(42, SeqCst);            // Total order over all threads

17.8 7. Atomics vs Mutex

17.8.1 Lock-Free Atomics

use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicU64, Ordering};

let counter = Arc::new(AtomicU64::new(0));

for _ in 0..100 {
    let counter_clone = Arc::clone(&counter);
    thread::spawn(move || {
        counter_clone.fetch_add(1, Ordering::SeqCst);  // No locks!
    });
}

// No contention, no blocking

17.8.2 Mutex-Based

use std::sync::Mutex;

let counter = Arc::new(Mutex::new(0u64));

for _ in 0..100 {
    let counter_clone = Arc::clone(&counter);
    thread::spawn(move || {
        let mut guard = counter_clone.lock().unwrap();
        *guard += 1;  // Locked
    });
}

// Contention possible, may block

17.8.3 Performance

AtomicU64::fetch_add: 1-2 cycles
Mutex::lock: 10-100 cycles (depending on contention)

17.9 8. Compare-and-Swap (CAS)

17.9.1 Atomic CAS

use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicU32, Ordering};

let expected = 10;
let new = 20;
let atomic = AtomicU32::new(10);

match atomic.compare_exchange(expected, new, Ordering::SeqCst, Ordering::Acquire) {
    Ok(old) => println!("Swapped: {} → {}", old, new),
    Err(actual) => println!("Failed: {} != {}", actual, expected),
}

17.9.2 Lock-Free Loops

use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicU32, Ordering};

let value = AtomicU32::new(0);

loop {
    let current = value.load(Ordering::Acquire);
    let new = current + 1;

    match value.compare_exchange(
        current,
        new,
        Ordering::Release,
        Ordering::Relaxed
    ) {
        Ok(_) => break,      // Success
        Err(_) => continue,  // Retry (another thread beat us)
    }
}

17.10 9. Thread-Local Storage

17.10.1 thread_local! Macro

thread_local! {
    static BUFFER: RefCell<Vec<u8>> = RefCell::new(Vec::new());
}

BUFFER.with(|buf| {
    buf.borrow_mut().push(42);
});

17.10.2 Implementation

Each thread has its own instance of BUFFER
No synchronization needed (no sharing)
Per-thread overhead: 8 bytes (pointer to thread-local data)

17.11 10. RwLock: Read-Write Synchronization

17.11.1 Multiple Readers, Single Writer

use std::sync::RwLock;

let data = RwLock::new(vec![1, 2, 3]);

// Multiple threads can read simultaneously
let read_guard1 = data.read().unwrap();
let read_guard2 = data.read().unwrap();

// Writer waits for all readers
// let write_guard = data.write().unwrap();  // Would block until readers drop

17.11.2 Reader-Writer State

17.12 11. Barrier Synchronization

17.12.1 Barrier

use std::sync::Barrier;

let barrier = Arc::new(Barrier::new(3));  // Wait for 3 threads

for _ in 0..3 {
    let barrier_clone = Arc::clone(&barrier);
    thread::spawn(move || {
        println!("Thread waiting");
        barrier_clone.wait();  // Wait for all 3
        println!("All threads reached");
    });
}

17.12.2 Barrier Execution

17.13 12. Thread Panic Propagation

17.13.1 Panic in Thread

let handle = thread::spawn(|| {
    panic!("Error!");
});

match handle.join() {
    Ok(_) => println!("Success"),
    Err(_) => println!("Thread panicked"),
}

17.13.2 Panic Isolation

Main thread:  [running]  [join]  [continue]
Worker thread:                   [panic!]  [unwind + exit]

Main thread is NOT affected by worker panic

17.14 13. Performance Characteristics

17.14.1 Overhead

Creating thread: 1-10 ms (OS scheduling)
Atomic operation: 1-10 cycles
Channel send: 50-500 cycles (depends on contention)
Mutex lock: 10-1000 cycles (uncontended to contended)
Context switch: 100-10,000 cycles

17.15 14. Anti-Patterns

17.15.1 WRONG: Sharing Rc

let data = Rc::new(42);  // NOT thread-safe!
let clone = Rc::clone(&data);

thread::spawn(move || {
    println!("{}", clone);  // ERROR: Rc not Send
});

17.15.2 CORRECT: Use Arc

let data = Arc::new(42);  // Thread-safe ref counting
let clone = Arc::clone(&data);

thread::spawn(move || {
    println!("{}", clone);  // OK: Arc is Send
});

17.16 Summary Diagram

18 Rayon: Data Parallelism with Work-Stealing Under the Hood

18.1 Overview

Rayon provides data-parallel abstractions using a work-stealing scheduler. Unlike Tokio (task-parallel, async), Rayon targets CPU-bound parallel computations with declarative API that parallelizes iterators automatically.

18.2 1. Parallelism vs Concurrency

18.2.1 Parallelism (Rayon)

use rayon::prelude::*;

let sum: i32 = (1..1000)
    .into_par_iter()
    .map(|x| x * x)
    .sum();

Characteristics: - Multiple threads execute simultaneously - Work on independent data - CPU-bound (compute-intensive) - Goal: utilize all CPU cores

18.2.2 Concurrency (Tokio)

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let fut1 = some_io_operation();
    let fut2 = some_io_operation();
    
    let (r1, r2) = tokio::join!(fut1, fut2);
}

Characteristics: - Single or few threads interleave work - Work on shared state - I/O-bound (I/O-intensive) - Goal: handle many concurrent operations

18.3 2. Rayon Work-Stealing Scheduler

18.3.1 Thread Pool

use rayon::prelude::*;

// Default: thread pool with CPU core count threads
let pool = rayon::ThreadPoolBuilder::new()
    .num_threads(4)  // Explicit control
    .build()
    .unwrap();

pool.install(|| {
    (0..100)
        .into_par_iter()
        .for_each(|i| println!("{}", i));
});

18.3.2 Work-Stealing Queue Structure

18.4 3. Iterator Parallelization

18.4.1 Sequential Iterator

let result: Vec<i32> = (0..1000)
    .iter()
    .map(|x| x * 2)
    .collect();

Execution: Single thread processes all 1000 elements sequentially.

18.4.2 Parallel Iterator

use rayon::prelude::*;

let result: Vec<i32> = (0..1000)
    .into_par_iter()
    .map(|x| x * 2)
    .collect();

Execution: Multiple threads work on chunks in parallel.

18.4.3 Compiler Transformation

18.5 4. Work Division Strategy

18.5.1 Divide and Conquer

(0..1000).into_par_iter().map(f).collect()

Thread pool with 4 threads:

Iteration 0-249:   Thread 0 (chunk 0)
Iteration 250-499: Thread 1 (chunk 1)
Iteration 500-749: Thread 2 (chunk 2)
Iteration 750-999: Thread 3 (chunk 3)

18.5.2 Dynamic Load Balancing

Initial state:
  Thread 0: [chunk0: 250 tasks]  ← Busy
  Thread 1: [chunk1: 250 tasks]  ← Busy
  Thread 2: [chunk2: 250 tasks]  ← Busy
  Thread 3: [chunk3: 250 tasks]  ← Busy

If Thread 0 finishes early:
  Thread 0: []                    ← Idle
  → Steals work from Thread 1
  → Now helps finish Thread 1's chunk

Result: Better CPU utilization than naive chunking.

18.6 5. Join and Fork

18.6.1 Explicit Parallelism

use rayon::prelude::*;

let (left, right) = rayon::join(
    || expensive_left_computation(),
    || expensive_right_computation()
);
// left and right computed in parallel

18.6.2 join() Implementation

18.7 6. Divide and Conquer Example

18.7.1 Merge Sort with Rayon

fn merge_sort(v: &mut [i32]) {
    if v.len() <= 1000 {
        // Base case: sort sequentially (small)
        v.sort();
    } else {
        let mid = v.len() / 2;
        rayon::join(
            || merge_sort(&mut v[..mid]),
            || merge_sort(&mut v[mid..])
        );
        // Merge halves
    }
}

Parallel execution tree:

                [full array]
                /          \
         (parallel)      (parallel)
           /                    \
      [left half]           [right half]
       /      \              /      \
      /        \            /        \
    ...       ...         ...        ...
    
At leaf (1000 elements): sequential sort
Then merge back up the tree in parallel

18.8 7. Thread Safety and Scope

18.8.1 Scope Guards Ownership

let mut data = vec![1, 2, 3];

rayon::scope(|s| {
    s.spawn(|_| {
        // Can capture &mut data safely
        data[0] = 10;
    });
    s.spawn(|_| {
        data[1] = 20;
    });
    // Scope waits for all spawns to complete before returning
});

println!("{:?}", data);  // [10, 20, 3]

Safety mechanism:

18.9 8. Reduction and Combine

18.9.1 Parallel Reduce

use rayon::prelude::*;

let sum: i32 = (1..1000)
    .into_par_iter()
    .reduce(|| 0, |a, b| a + b);

Execution model:

[1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8]

Thread 0: 1+2+3+4 = 10
Thread 1: 5+6+7+8 = 26
Main:    10+26 = 36

18.9.2 Tree Reduction (binary tree combine)

18.10 9. Rayon vs Tokio

18.10.1 Comparison

18.11 10. Memory Model

18.11.1 No Shared State Mutations (Usually)

// Safe: each thread has its own closure
(0..1000)
    .into_par_iter()
    .for_each(|i| {
        let local_var = i * 2;  // Thread-local
        println!("{}", local_var);  // No races
    });

18.11.2 Shared State with Thread-Safe Types

use std::sync::atomic::AtomicU64;
use std::sync::Arc;

let counter = Arc::new(AtomicU64::new(0));

(0..1000)
    .into_par_iter()
    .for_each(|_| {
        counter.fetch_add(1, Relaxed);  // Thread-safe atomic
    });

18.12 11. Performance Characteristics

18.12.1 When Rayon Excels

Parallel sum of 1 million numbers:
Seq:   1000 ms
Par:   250 ms (4 threads)
Speedup: 4× (near-linear!)

Reason: CPU-bound, embarrassingly parallel

18.12.2 When Rayon Struggles

Parallel: send value over channel:
Seq:   100 ns
Par:   10 μs (contention on lock-free queue!)
Slowdown: 100×

Reason: Too much synchronization overhead

18.13 12. Example: Parallel Map Reduce

use rayon::prelude::*;
use std::collections::HashMap;

let data = vec![1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8];

// Parallel map
let counts: Vec<(i32, usize)> = data
    .into_par_iter()
    .map(|x| (x, 1))
    .collect();

// Parallel reduce to combine
let result: HashMap<i32, usize> = counts
    .into_par_iter()
    .reduce(
        HashMap::new,
        |mut map, (k, v)| {
            *map.entry(k).or_insert(0) += v;
            map
        }
    );

18.14 13. Overhead and When to Use

18.14.1 Overhead

Spawning a task: ~1-10 μs
Stealing work: ~100 ns

Only parallelize if:
- Task > 10 μs of work
- Multiple tasks with good locality

18.14.2 Decision Tree

18.15 14. Thread Pool Internals

18.15.1 Stealing Algorithm

If local_queue is not empty:
  Pop task from local_queue
  Execute task
Else (idle):
  For each other thread:
    Try to steal from other.queue
    If successful: execute
    Else: continue to next
  If nothing stolen:
    Thread parks (waits for work)

18.15.2 Wake-up

When new work enqueued:
1. Check for idle threads
2. Wake one thread (unpark)
3. Woken thread dequeues work
4. Other threads steal as needed

18.16 Summary

Aspect Rayon Tokio
Best for CPU-bound parallelism I/O-bound concurrency
Scheduling Work-stealing Event-driven
Threads One per CPU core Configurable
Blocking Allowed (efficient) Problematic (starves executor)
Scalability O(cores) O(tasks)

Next: Concurrency & Threads → Learn threading, channels, atomics.

19 Tokio Async Runtime: I/O Multiplexing and Scheduling Under the Hood

19.1 Overview

Tokio is an asynchronous runtime built on top of Rust’s Future trait. It provides sophisticated I/O multiplexing, work-stealing schedulers, and efficient resource management—all to enable high-concurrency applications with minimal overhead.

19.2 1. What is a Runtime?

19.2.1 The Runtime’s Job

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    // Runtime manages:
    // 1. Spawning and scheduling tasks
    // 2. Polling futures to completion
    // 3. I/O notifications (epoll, kqueue, IOCP)
    // 4. Timers and timeouts
}

Without runtime: Futures sit idle. Nobody calls poll().

With Tokio runtime: Futures are continuously polled until completion.

19.3 2. Tokio Architecture

19.3.1 High-Level Design

19.4 3. Work-Stealing Scheduler

19.4.1 Problem: Load Balancing

Thread 1: Busy with heavy task
Thread 2: Idle, nothing to do

Result: CPU 2 is wasted!

19.4.2 Solution: Work Stealing

Thread 1: Busy
Thread 2: Idle → "Steal" a task from Thread 1's queue

Result: Both threads busy!

Implementation:

19.4.3 Work Queue Structure

19.5 4. I/O Multiplexing

19.5.1 The Challenge

1000 concurrent connections
→ Can't create 1000 threads (too expensive)
→ Need single thread to monitor ALL connections

Solution: I/O multiplexing (epoll, kqueue, IOCP)

19.5.2 Epoll (Linux)

// Conceptual epoll usage:
let epoll_fd = epoll_create();

// Register socket for reading
epoll_ctl(epoll_fd, socket_fd, EPOLLIN);

// Wait for events:
epoll_wait(epoll_fd, events, timeout);
// Returns when: socket readable, timeout, or signal

19.5.3 Event Notification Flow

19.5.4 Multiplexing Efficiency

Without multiplexing (thread per connection):
- 1000 connections → 1000 threads
- Stack per thread: 2 MB
- Memory: 2 GB just for stacks!
- Context switching: O(n) overhead

With I/O multiplexing (1 thread, 1000 connections):
- Stack: 2 MB (single thread)
- Scheduling: O(connections with events) overhead
- epoll_wait: O(1) notification for readiness

19.6 5. Timer Wheel

19.6.1 Problem: Many Timeouts

tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_secs(10)).await;  // 10,000 tasks with timeouts

Naive approach: sorted list
→ Insert: O(n), check expiry: O(n)
→ Thousands of timeouts → slow!

19.6.2 Solution: Timer Wheel (Ring Buffer)

Slot 0: Tasks expiring now
Slot 1: Tasks expiring in 1 ms
Slot 2: Tasks expiring in 2 ms
...
Slot 999: Tasks expiring in 999 ms

Each ms: advance pointer, wake all in slot
Insert: O(1)
Check: O(1) per advancing tick

Visualization:

19.7 6. Task Spawning

19.7.1 Spawn a Task

tokio::spawn(async {
    // Runs independently on thread pool
});

19.7.2 Internal Flow

19.8 7. Runtime Configuration

19.8.1 Default Runtime

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    // Multi-threaded runtime
    // Threads = CPU cores
    // Work-stealing enabled
}

19.8.2 Single-Threaded

#[tokio::main(flavor = "current_thread")]
async fn main() {
    // Single thread only
    // Simpler, less overhead
    // No work-stealing (unnecessary)
}

19.8.3 Tuning

use tokio::runtime;

let rt = runtime::Builder::new_multi_thread()
    .worker_threads(4)  // Number of threads
    .thread_name("worker")
    .build()?;

rt.block_on(async {
    // Run async code
});

19.9 8. Blocking Operations

19.9.1 Problem: CPU-Bound Work

async fn process_data() {
    let result = expensive_computation();  // Blocks executor!
    // While this thread is blocked, other tasks can't progress
}

19.9.2 Solution: block_in_place

async fn process_data() {
    let result = tokio::task::block_in_place(|| {
        expensive_computation()  // Blocks, but scheduler handles it
    });
}

Internal handling: 1. Current thread signals: “I’m going to block” 2. Scheduler spins up replacement thread 3. Block completes 4. Continue on any available thread

19.10 9. Channels

19.10.1 MPSC (Multiple Producer, Single Consumer)

let (tx, mut rx) = tokio::sync::mpsc::channel(100);

tokio::spawn(async move {
    tx.send(42).await;
});

if let Some(val) = rx.recv().await {
    println!("{}", val);
}

19.10.2 Implementation

19.11 10. Efficiency Characteristics

19.11.1 Memory Usage

Per task:
- Future state: depends on async fn (typically 100-1000 bytes)
- Task metadata: 64 bytes
- No separate stack (stack-based state machine)

1 million tasks: 100 MB - 1 GB (reasonable!)
1 million threads: 2 TB (impossible!)

19.11.2 CPU Efficiency

Operations per task per scheduler iteration:
1. Dequeue task: O(1)
2. Poll future: O(1) - depends on async operation
3. Re-queue if Pending: O(1)

Total: O(1) per operation

19.12 11. Tokio Task Model

19.12.1 Task vs Future

// Future: just a computation
let fut = async { 42 };

// Task: Future + metadata
tokio::spawn(async { 42 });  // Wraps in Task

Task includes: - Future itself - JoinHandle (for await task completion) - Cancel token (for cancellation) - Local storage (task-local data)

19.13 12. Example: TCP Server Architecture

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let listener = TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:8080").await?;

    loop {
        let (socket, addr) = listener.accept().await?;
        tokio::spawn(async move {
            handle_client(socket, addr).await
        });
    }
}

Runtime execution:

19.14 13. Performance Comparison

19.14.1 Sync vs Async

Sync Server (threads):
- 1000 connections → 1000 threads
- Context switches: O(n) = 1000 switches per time slice
- Memory: 2 GB (1000 × 2 MB stacks)

Async Server (Tokio):
- 1000 connections → 1 thread pool (4-8 threads)
- Context switches: O(m) = 4-8 switches per time slice
- Memory: 2 MB (single thread stacks)
- Throughput: 100-1000× higher

19.15 14. Debugging and Monitoring

19.15.1 Tracing Integration

use tracing::instrument;

#[instrument]
async fn my_function() {
    // Automatic span created
}

19.15.2 Metrics

// Can track:
- Active tasks
- Scheduled tasks
- Work-stealing operations
- I/O events per second

19.16 Summary: Tokio Magic

Component Purpose Technique
Scheduler Fair task distribution Work-stealing
I/O Multiplexing Monitor thousands of fds epoll/kqueue
Timer Wheel Efficient timeouts Ring buffer
Task Queue Store pending work Lock-free deque

Next: Rayon Parallelism → Learn data-parallelism with work-stealing.

20 Macros: Metaprogramming and Code Generation Under the Hood

20.1 Overview

Rust macros are code generation systems that expand at compile time before type checking. Two types exist: declarative macros (pattern matching) and procedural macros (functions that manipulate token trees).

20.2 1. Declarative Macros (Macro Rules)

20.2.1 Simple Macro Definition

macro_rules! println {
    ($($arg:tt)*) => {
        $crate::io::_print($crate::format_args!($($arg)*));
    };
}

20.2.2 Macro Expansion Process

20.2.3 Macro Rules Syntax

macro_rules! my_macro {
    () => {
        // Rule 1: Match zero arguments
    };
    ($a:expr) => {
        // Rule 2: Match one expression
    };
    ($($item:item)*) => {
        // Rule 3: Match zero or more items
    };
}

20.3 2. Token Trees

20.3.1 What Are Tokens?

println!("hello", x, y + 2);

// Tokens:
// - Identifier: println
// - Punctuation: !
// - Literal: "hello"
// - Punctuation: ,
// - Identifier: x
// - Punctuation: ,
// - Identifier: y
// - Punctuation: +
// - Literal: 2
// - Punctuation: ;

20.3.2 Macro Input: Token Stream

20.4 3. Capture Groups and Repetition

20.4.1 Capture Syntax

macro_rules! repeat {
    ($item:expr, $($repeat:expr),*) => {
        // $item matches one expression
        // $($repeat),* matches comma-separated expressions
        // * = zero or more
        // + = one or more
        // ? = zero or one
    };
}

repeat!(value, a, b, c, d);  // item=value, repeat=[a,b,c,d]

20.4.2 Repetition Semantics

macro_rules! repeat_expand {
    ($($item:expr),*) => {
        // $($item),* expands to:
        // If input: a, b, c
        // Output: a, b, c (same)
        // The * repeats the entire group
    };
}

repeat_expand!(1, 2, 3);
// Expands to: 1, 2, 3

20.5 4. Fragment Specifiers

20.5.1 Available Types

20.5.2 Using Fragment Specifiers

macro_rules! example {
    ($e:expr) => { /* ... */ };          // Matches expressions
    ($ty:ty) => { /* ... */ };           // Matches types
    ($id:ident) => { /* ... */ };        // Matches identifiers
    ($item:item) => { /* ... */ };       // Matches items (fn, struct, etc)
}

20.6 5. Macro Expansion Example

20.6.1 Input Code

vec![1, 2, 3];

20.6.2 Vec Macro Definition (Simplified)

macro_rules! vec {
    ($($element:expr),*) => {
        {
            let mut _v = Vec::new();
            $(_v.push($element);)*
            _v
        }
    };
}

20.6.3 Expansion Process

Input tokens: [ 1, 2, 3 ]

Match rule: ($($element:expr),*)
Capture: $element = [1, 2, 3]

Substitute in template:
{
    let mut _v = Vec::new();
    _v.push(1);
    _v.push(2);
    _v.push(3);
    _v
}

Final code (type-checked):
{
    let mut _v: Vec<_> = Vec::new();
    _v.push(1);
    _v.push(2);
    _v.push(3);
    _v
}

20.7 6. Procedural Macros

20.7.1 Three Types

20.8 7. Procedural Macro Implementation

20.8.1 Function-Like Procedural Macro

use proc_macro::TokenStream;

#[proc_macro]
pub fn sql(input: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
    // Parse token stream
    let sql_string = input.to_string();
    
    // Analyze SQL
    let analysis = analyze_sql(&sql_string);
    
    // Generate code
    quote! {
        PreparedStatement::new(#sql_string)
    }.into()
}

20.8.2 Derive Macro

#[proc_macro_derive(MyTrait)]
pub fn derive_my_trait(input: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
    // Parse the struct/enum
    let item = parse_macro_input!(input as DeriveInput);
    
    // Generate implementation
    let name = &item.ident;
    quote! {
        impl MyTrait for #name {
            // Auto-generated methods
        }
    }.into()
}

20.9 8. Macro Hygiene

20.9.1 Hygiene Problem (Accidental Capture)

macro_rules! bad_macro {
    ($body:expr) => {
        let x = 1;
        $body  // If $body contains x, it's captured!
    };
}

let x = 10;
bad_macro!(println!("{}", x));  // Prints 1, not 10!

20.9.2 Hygiene Solution

// Rust 2.0+ macro hygiene prevents accidental capture
// Variables from macro are "marked" as from macro context
// Outer x and inner x are in different scopes

20.9.3 Gensym (Generated Symbols)

macro_rules! avoid_collision {
    () => {
        let __internal_var = 1;  // Unlikely to conflict
        // Or use quasi-quotation system in procedural macros
    };
}

20.10 9. Quote and Quasi-Quotation

20.10.1 quote! Macro (Procedural)

use quote::quote;

let name = syn::parse_str::<syn::Ident>("MyStruct")?;
let expanded = quote! {
    impl Default for #name {
        fn default() -> Self {
            Self { /* ... */ }
        }
    }
};

// Generated code with interpolation (#name)

20.10.2 Interpolation

let field_name = "x";
let field_type = quote! { i32 };

let generated = quote! {
    pub #field_name: #field_type,
};

// Produces: pub x: i32,

20.11 10. Common Macro Patterns

20.11.1 Assert Macro

macro_rules! assert {
    ($cond:expr) => {
        if !($cond) {
            panic!("assertion failed: {}", stringify!($cond))
        }
    };
}

// stringify! converts token tree to string

20.11.2 Debug Print Macro

macro_rules! dbg {
    ($val:expr) => {
        eprintln!("[{}:{}] {} = {:#?}", file!(), line!(), stringify!($val), $val)
    };
}

// file!() → current file name
// line!() → current line number
// stringify!() → convert tokens to string

20.12 11. Performance: Macros vs Functions

20.12.1 Macro Overhead

Macro expansion: Happens at compile time (no runtime cost)
Code generation: Can produce inline-able code
Result: Often better than function (inlining opportunity)

20.12.2 Comparison

// Macro (likely inlined):
macro_rules! add {
    ($a:expr, $b:expr) => { $a + $b };
}
let r = add!(x, y);  // Inlined as: x + y

// Function (might not inline):
fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 { a + b }
let r = add(x, y);   // May generate function call

20.13 12. Limitations of Macros

20.13.1 Cannot Access Types

macro_rules! bad {
    ($val:expr) => {
        // No way to know type of $val at compile time!
        println!("{}", std::mem::size_of_val(&$val));  // WRONG
    };
}

20.13.2 Solution: Procedural Macros

#[proc_macro]
pub fn size_of(input: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
    // Parse the type
    let ty = parse_macro_input!(input as syn::Type);
    
    // Can access type information!
    quote! {
        std::mem::size_of::<#ty>()
    }.into()
}

20.14 13. Macro Debugging

20.14.1 Expand Macros (cargo expand)

cargo install cargo-expand
cargo expand  # Shows generated code

20.14.2 Manual Inspection

// Use println! in macro to debug expansion
macro_rules! debug_macro {
    ($x:expr) => {
        println!("Expanded with: {}", stringify!($x));
        $x
    };
}

20.15 14. Built-in Macros

20.15.1 Compile-Time Constants

file!()      // Current file name
line!()      // Current line number
column!()    // Current column
module_path!() // Current module path
stringify!() // Convert tokens to string
concat!()    // Concatenate strings (compile-time)
env!()       // Environment variable

20.15.2 Conditional Compilation

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests { }

#[cfg(unix)]
fn unix_only() { }

#[cfg_attr(doc, doc = "...")]
pub struct S;

20.16 Summary

Aspect Declarative Procedural
Define macro_rules! #[proc_macro]
Pattern Matching Yes No (uses Syn crate)
Type Access No Yes (via Syn)
Hygiene Automatic Manual (quote!)
Learning Curve Moderate Steep

Next: Optimization → Learn compiler optimizations and zero-cost abstractions.

21 Optimization: Compiler Optimizations and Zero-Cost Abstractions

21.1 Overview

Rust abstractions (generics, traits, closures) compile away, producing the same machine code as hand-optimized C. Understanding optimizations helps write efficient code and predict performance.

21.2 1. Inlining

21.2.1 What is Inlining?

fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 {
    a + b
}

let result = add(x, y);

21.2.2 Without Inlining (Unoptimized)

call add        ; Call function
; add function:
add rax, rbx    ; Add values
ret             ; Return

21.2.3 With Inlining (Optimized)

add rax, rbx    ; Add values directly (no call!)

Result: 10-50 CPU cycles saved per call elimination.

21.2.4 Inline Hints

#[inline]       // Hint: inline this
#[inline(never)]  // Never inline
#[inline(always)] // Always inline (weak hint)

pub fn inlined() { }       // Default: compiler decides
pub fn never_inline() { }  // Prevent inlining

21.3 2. Monomorphization Optimization

21.3.1 Specialization

fn identity<T>(x: T) -> T {
    x
}

let i = identity(42);     // Generates: identity_i32
let s = identity("hello"); // Generates: identity_str

21.3.2 Code Generation

21.3.3 LLVM Optimization

identity_i32(x):
  return x           ; x in rax, direct return

identity_String(x):
  return x           ; x in rdi (pointer), direct return

Result: Zero overhead over manual specialization.

21.4 3. Dead Code Elimination

21.4.1 Unused Code Removal

fn unused() {
    let x = expensive_computation();  // Never used
}

fn caller() {
    unused();  // Function called but side effects removed
}

21.4.2 Optimization Result

; Dead code eliminated entirely!
caller:
    ret        ; Function is now a no-op

21.5 4. Loop Unrolling

21.5.1 Small Loops

for i in 0..4 {
    buffer[i] = i as u8;
}

21.5.2 Unrolled Version

mov byte [buffer + 0], 0
mov byte [buffer + 1], 1
mov byte [buffer + 2], 2
mov byte [buffer + 3], 3

Result: No loop overhead for small, known-size loops.

21.6 5. Vectorization (SIMD)

21.6.1 Auto-Vectorization

for i in 0..1000 {
    result[i] = a[i] + b[i];  // Can be vectorized
}

21.6.2 Vectorized Code

movdqa xmm0, [a + 0]    ; Load 4 i32s
movdqa xmm1, [b + 0]    ; Load 4 i32s
paddd xmm0, xmm1        ; Add 4 values simultaneously
movdqa [result], xmm0   ; Store 4 results

Result: 4× faster (on SSE), 8× with AVX2.

21.7 6. Branch Prediction

21.7.1 Predictable Branches

for item in items {
    if item.valid {        // Usually true
        process(item);
    }
}

21.7.2 Compiler Optimization

cmp rax, 0              ; Check if valid
jne .process            ; Branch (likely to be taken)
jmp .next_item

.process:
    call process
.next_item:
    ; Continue loop

Prediction: CPU guesses which way branch goes. Correct guess = no penalty. Wrong guess = 20+ cycle stall.

21.7.3 Branch Hints (Unstable)

if core::intrinsics::likely(condition) {
    // Hint to compiler: this branch is usually taken
}

21.8 7. Constant Folding

21.8.1 Compile-Time Computation

const BUFFER_SIZE: usize = 4 * 1024;  // Computed at compile time
const TAU: f64 = 2.0 * std::f64::consts::PI;  // Folded to constant

21.8.2 Result

mov rax, 4096    ; Constant directly in code

Cost: Zero runtime overhead.

21.9 8. Function Pointer Optimization

21.9.1 Virtual Function Calls (Vtable)

trait Animal { fn speak(&self); }

fn call_animal(a: &dyn Animal) {
    a.speak();  // Dynamic dispatch (vtable lookup)
}

21.9.2 Monomorphization (Devirtualization)

fn call_animal<T: Animal>(a: &T) {
    a.speak();  // Static dispatch (inline-able!)
}

call_animal(&dog);   // Can inline Dog::speak()
call_animal(&cat);   // Can inline Cat::speak()

Compiler can devirtualize when concrete type known.

21.10 9. Escape Analysis

21.10.1 Stack vs Heap

// Without escape analysis (pessimistic):
let v = Vec::new();
let ptr = Box::new(v);  // Allocates unnecessarily

// With escape analysis (optimistic):
// Compiler sees v never escapes Box
// Optimizes to stack allocation

21.10.2 Scalar Replacement of Aggregates

struct Point { x: i32, y: i32 }

let p = Point { x: 10, y: 20 };
let x = p.x;

21.10.3 Optimized

mov rax, 10    ; x directly in register
; Point struct eliminated

21.11 10. Inlining and Specialization Trade-offs

21.11.1 Code Size vs Speed

21.12 11. LTO: Link-Time Optimization

21.12.1 Whole-Program Optimization

# Cargo.toml
[profile.release]
lto = true      # Enable LTO (slower compile, faster binary)
codegen-units = 1  # Single codegen unit (better optimization)

21.12.2 LTO Benefits

Without LTO:
- Each crate compiled independently
- Can't inline across crates

With LTO:
- Link time: Entire program re-optimized
- Can inline across crate boundaries
- 5-20% faster binaries (at cost of compile time)

21.13 12. SIMD Intrinsics

21.13.1 Manual SIMD Optimization

use std::arch::x86_64::*;

unsafe fn add_vectors(a: &[f32], b: &[f32]) -> Vec<f32> {
    let mut result = vec![0.0; a.len()];
    
    for i in (0..a.len()).step_by(4) {
        let av = _mm_loadu_ps(&a[i]);    // Load 4 floats
        let bv = _mm_loadu_ps(&b[i]);    // Load 4 floats
        let sum = _mm_add_ps(av, bv);    // Add 4 at once
        _mm_storeu_ps(&mut result[i], sum); // Store 4 results
    }
    
    result
}

Result: 4-8× faster than scalar loop.

21.14 13. Profile-Guided Optimization (PGO)

21.14.1 Using PGO

# Profile: run program to collect data
RUSTFLAGS="-C profile-use=profiles/default.profraw" cargo build -O

# Optimize with profile data
RUSTFLAGS="-C llvm-args=-pgo-warn-missing-function" cargo build -O

Compiler optimizes based on actual runtime patterns.

21.15 14. Benchmarking

21.15.1 Criterion Benchmarking

use criterion::{black_box, criterion_group, criterion_main, Criterion};

fn fibonacci(n: u32) -> u32 {
    match n {
        0 | 1 => 1,
        _ => fibonacci(n - 1) + fibonacci(n - 2),
    }
}

fn criterion_benchmark(c: &mut Criterion) {
    c.bench_function("fib 10", |b| {
        b.iter(|| fibonacci(black_box(10)))  // black_box prevents optimization
    });
}

criterion_group!(benches, criterion_benchmark);
criterion_main!(benches);

21.15.2 Black Box

black_box(x)  // Prevent compiler from optimizing away computation

21.16 15. Compiler Flags for Optimization

21.16.1 Release Profile

[profile.release]
opt-level = 3           # 0-3, or "z" for size
lto = true              # Link-time optimization
codegen-units = 1       # Single unit for better optimization
strip = true            # Strip debug symbols

21.16.2 Debug Profile

[profile.dev]
opt-level = 0           # Fast compilation
debug = true            # Include debug symbols

21.16.3 Custom Profile

[profile.profiling]
inherits = "release"
debug = true            # Keep debug info in release

21.17 16. Zero-Cost Abstraction Examples

21.17.1 Iterator Abstractions

// High-level
let sum: i32 = (0..1000)
    .map(|x| x * 2)
    .filter(|x| x % 3 == 0)
    .sum();

// Compiles to:
let mut sum = 0;
for i in 0..1000 {
    let x = i * 2;
    if x % 3 == 0 {
        sum += x;
    }
}

Result: Identical machine code (iterators eliminated).

21.18 17. Common Optimization Pitfalls

21.18.1 WRONG: Over-Optimizing

// Premature optimization
let v: Vec<u32> = vec![1, 2, 3];
let cached_len = v.len();  // Caching length (compiler optimizes this anyway!)

21.18.2 CORRECT: Trust Compiler

let v: Vec<u32> = vec![1, 2, 3];
for i in 0..v.len() {
    // Compiler optimizes v.len() to constant
}

21.19 Summary

Optimization When Overhead
Inlining Small functions 0 (saves CPU cycles)
Monomorphization Generics 0 (replaces monomorphic)
Dead code elimination Unused 0 (removes)
Vectorization Simple loops 4-8× faster
LTO Whole program 10-20% faster (slower compile)

Next: Advanced Topics → Learn unsafe, FFI, SIMD, allocators, const generics.

22 Advanced Topics: Unsafe, FFI, SIMD, Allocators, Const Generics

22.1 Overview

Advanced Rust features enable systems programming: unsafe bypasses borrow checker (with responsibility), FFI calls C/C++ code, SIMD exploits hardware parallelism, custom allocators control memory management, and const generics add compile-time parameters.

22.2 1. Unsafe Blocks

22.2.1 Unsafe Capabilities

unsafe {
    // 1. Dereference raw pointers
    let ptr: *const i32 = &42;
    let value = *ptr;

    // 2. Call unsafe functions
    libc::printf(b"Hello\n");

    // 3. Mutate static variables
    static mut COUNTER: u32 = 0;
    COUNTER += 1;

    // 4. Implement unsafe traits
    // impl UnsafeTrait for MyType { }
}

22.2.2 Safety Invariants (Programmer’s Responsibility)

unsafe fn dereference_option(ptr: Option<&i32>) -> i32 {
    // SAFETY: Option is non-null, so unwrap_unchecked is safe
    *ptr.unwrap_unchecked()
}

22.3 2. Raw Pointers

22.3.1 Creating Raw Pointers

let x = 42;
let ptr_imm: *const i32 = &x as *const i32;     // Immutable
let mut y = 10;
let ptr_mut: *mut i32 = &mut y as *mut i32;    // Mutable

22.3.2 Dereferencing Raw Pointers

unsafe {
    *ptr_mut = 20;           // Dereference mutable
    let val = *ptr_imm;      // Dereference immutable
}

22.3.3 Pointer Arithmetic

unsafe {
    let arr = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
    let ptr = arr.as_ptr();
    
    let elem0 = *ptr;           // arr[0]
    let elem1 = *(ptr.add(1));  // arr[1]
}

22.4 3. FFI: Foreign Function Interface

22.4.1 Calling C Code

extern "C" {
    fn strlen(s: *const u8) -> usize;
}

fn get_length(s: &str) -> usize {
    unsafe {
        strlen(s.as_ptr())
    }
}

22.4.2 Memory Layout Guarantees

use std::ffi::CStr;

#[repr(C)]
struct Point {
    x: i32,
    y: i32,
}

// #[repr(C)] ensures C-compatible memory layout
// Without it: field ordering might differ

22.4.3 Calling Convention

extern "C" fn rust_callback(value: i32) -> i32 {
    value * 2
}

// extern "C" uses C calling convention
// Allows C code to call Rust functions

22.4.4 C String Handling

use std::ffi::{CStr, CString};

// Rust String → C string (null-terminated)
let c_str = CString::new("hello").unwrap();
let c_ptr: *const i8 = c_str.as_ptr();

unsafe {
    // C string → Rust String
    let c_str_ref = CStr::from_ptr(c_ptr);
    let rust_str = c_str_ref.to_str().unwrap();
}

22.5 4. SIMD Intrinsics

22.5.1 SSE/AVX Operations

#[cfg(target_arch = "x86_64")]
use std::arch::x86_64::*;

fn vector_add(a: &[f32; 4], b: &[f32; 4]) -> [f32; 4] {
    unsafe {
        let av = _mm_loadu_ps(a.as_ptr());    // Load 4 floats
        let bv = _mm_loadu_ps(b.as_ptr());    // Load 4 floats
        let sum = _mm_add_ps(av, bv);         // Add (4 at once)
        
        let mut result = [0.0; 4];
        _mm_storeu_ps(result.as_mut_ptr(), sum); // Store 4 floats
        result
    }
}

22.5.2 SIMD Performance

22.5.3 Portable SIMD (Unstable)

#![feature(portable_simd)]

use std::simd::*;

fn vector_add(a: [f32; 4], b: [f32; 4]) -> [f32; 4] {
    let av = Simd::from_array(a);
    let bv = Simd::from_array(b);
    (av + bv).to_array()  // Compiler generates SIMD
}

22.6 5. Global Allocators

22.6.1 Custom Allocator

use std::alloc::{GlobalAlloc, Layout};

struct MyAllocator;

unsafe impl GlobalAlloc for MyAllocator {
    unsafe fn alloc(&self, layout: Layout) -> *mut u8 {
        // Custom allocation logic
        libc::malloc(layout.size()) as *mut u8
    }

    unsafe fn dealloc(&self, ptr: *mut u8, _layout: Layout) {
        libc::free(ptr as *mut libc::c_void);
    }
}

#[global_allocator]
static GLOBAL: MyAllocator = MyAllocator;

22.6.2 Allocator Trait

unsafe impl GlobalAlloc for MyAllocator {
    unsafe fn alloc(&self, layout: Layout) -> *mut u8 { ... }
    unsafe fn dealloc(&self, ptr: *mut u8, layout: Layout) { ... }
    unsafe fn realloc(&self, ptr: *mut u8, old: Layout, new: Layout) -> *mut u8 { ... }
}

22.7 6. Memory-Mapped I/O

22.7.1 Mmap Example

use std::os::unix::io::AsRawFd;

unsafe fn mmap_file(file: &std::fs::File, size: usize) -> *mut u8 {
    libc::mmap(
        std::ptr::null_mut(),
        size,
        libc::PROT_READ | libc::PROT_WRITE,
        libc::MAP_SHARED,
        file.as_raw_fd(),
        0
    ) as *mut u8
}

22.8 7. Const Generics

22.8.1 Const Parameters

fn array_sum<const N: usize>(arr: [i32; N]) -> i32 {
    arr.iter().sum()
}

let sum = array_sum([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]);  // N = 5

22.8.2 Const Evaluation

22.8.3 Benefits

// Without const generics (slow):
fn make_vec(size: usize) -> Vec<i32> {
    vec![0; size]  // Runtime allocation
}

// With const generics (fast):
fn make_array<const N: usize>() -> [i32; N] {
    [0; N]  // Stack allocation
}

22.9 8. Volatile Operations

22.9.1 Preventing Compiler Optimizations

use std::ptr;

let x = 42;
let ptr = &x as *const i32;

unsafe {
    let val = ptr::read_volatile(ptr);  // Can't optimize away
}

22.9.2 Use Cases

// Memory-mapped register (real hardware)
unsafe {
    let reg = 0xFFFF0000 as *mut u32;
    ptr::write_volatile(reg, value);  // Must write (can't optimize away)
}

22.10 9. Intrinsics

22.10.1 LLVM Intrinsics

extern "llvm_intrinsic" {
    fn llvm_x86_sse2_paddd_128(a: i32x4, b: i32x4) -> i32x4;
}

unsafe {
    let sum = llvm_x86_sse2_paddd_128(a, b);
}

22.10.2 Compiler Intrinsics

use core::intrinsics::*;

unsafe {
    rotate_left(value, bits);     // CPU rotate instruction
    unchecked_add(a, b);           // Addition without overflow check
    abort();                       // Immediate abort
}

22.11 10. Inline Assembly

22.11.1 asm! Macro

use std::arch::asm;

fn add_one(mut x: i32) -> i32 {
    unsafe {
        asm!(
            "add {0}, 1",
            inout(reg) x,
        );
    }
    x
}

// Generates: add eax, 1

22.11.2 Operand Constraints

unsafe {
    asm!(
        "add {0}, {1}",
        inout(reg) dst,     // inout = read and write
        in(reg) src,        // in = read only
    );
}

22.12 11. Type Safety in Unsafe Code

22.12.1 Soundness vs Type Safety

// Type-safe but unsound:
unsafe fn transmute_wrong<T, U>(t: T) -> U {
    std::mem::transmute(t)  // Reinterpret bytes (unsound!)
}

// This breaks safety if:
let ptr: *const i32 = transmute_wrong::<_, _>(&42.0);  // Wrong size!

22.12.2 Correct Unsafe Code

// Sound:
unsafe fn transmute_correct<T, U>(t: T) -> U
where
    T: Copy,
    U: Copy,
{
    if std::mem::size_of::<T>() != std::mem::size_of::<U>() {
        panic!("Size mismatch");  // Check at runtime
    }
    std::mem::transmute(t)
}

22.13 12. Unsafe Trait Implementation

22.13.1 Example: Marker Trait

unsafe trait UnsafeTrait {
    // Types implementing this must guarantee...
    // ...some property checked at compile time
}

unsafe impl UnsafeTrait for MyType {
    // Implementation must maintain invariants
    // Compiler trusts programmer
}

22.13.2 Example: Send Trait

// Manual Send implementation (usually auto-derived):
unsafe impl Send for MyPtr {
    // Compiler won't derive Send for custom types containing raw pointers
    // Programmer must implement to prove it's thread-safe
}

22.14 13. Advanced Memory Safety Patterns

22.14.1 Pinning

use std::pin::Pin;

fn requires_pin<T: Unpin>(t: Pin<&mut T>) {
    // t cannot be moved (even after unpinned)
}

22.14.2 Self-Referential Structs

struct SelfRef {
    data: i32,
    ptr_to_data: *const i32,  // Unsafe: points to own field
}

// Must use Pin to prevent moving
let s = Pin::new(Box::new(SelfRef { ... }));

22.15 14. Summary Table

Feature Safety Performance Use Case
Unsafe Programmer-checked Best FFI, atomics, optimization
FFI Interop-dependent Native C integration
SIMD Compiler-checked 4-8× faster Vector operations
Custom Allocator Allocator-dependent Customizable Specialized memory
Const Generics Compile-time Zero overhead Array sizes, compile-time math

22.16 15. Safe Abstractions over Unsafe

22.16.1 Example: SafeVec

pub struct SafeVec<T> {
    ptr: *mut T,
    cap: usize,
    len: usize,
}

impl<T> SafeVec<T> {
    pub fn push(&mut self, val: T) {
        unsafe {
            if self.len == self.cap {
                self.grow();
            }
            (*self.ptr.add(self.len)) = val;
            self.len += 1;
        }
    }

    pub fn get(&self, idx: usize) -> Option<&T> {
        if idx < self.len {
            unsafe { Some(&*self.ptr.add(idx)) }
        } else {
            None
        }
    }
}

// Safe interface hides unsafe internals
